asked: We make a brow tint, a lip gloss and a coal-tar-based permanent hair dye. How do FDA's color additive definitions treat 'area of the eye', 'externally applied' and the hair dye exemption?
answer:
The FDA's color additive definitions treat 'area of the eye' as defined in 21 CFR 70.3(s) to include the eyelids, eyebrows, and surrounding tissue; 'externally applied' means drugs or cosmetics applied only to external body parts excluding lips and mucous-covered surfaces per 21 CFR 70.3(v); and for coal-tar-based permanent hair dyes (which are not color additives), these provisions do not address a general exemption as they pertain specifically to chromium hydroxide green, a color additive with certification exemption under 21 CFR 73.2326(d).

21 CFR 70.3(s) [5] defines the term "area of the eye" as the area enclosed within the circumference of the supra-orbital ridge and the infra-orbital ridge, including the eyebrow, the skin below the eyebrow, the eyelids and the eyelashes, and conjunctival sac of the eye, the eyeball, and the soft areolar tissue that lies within the perimeter of the infra-orbital ridge.

21 CFR 70.3(v) [6] defines "externally applied drugs and externally applied cosmetics" as drugs or cosmetics applied only to external parts of the body and not to the lips or any body surface covered by mucous membrane.

21 CFR 73.2326(a) [1] specifies that chromium hydroxide green must conform in identity and specifications to § 73.1326 (a)(1) and (b).

21 CFR 73.2326(b) [2] states that chromium hydroxide green is safe for use in coloring externally applied cosmetics, including those intended for use in the area of the eye, in amounts consistent with good manufacturing practice.

21 CFR 73.2326(c) [3] requires labeling for chromium hydroxide green and any mixture prepared therefrom intended solely or in part for coloring purposes to bear labeling in accordance with § 70.25.

21 CFR 73.2326(d) [4] exempts certification of chromium hydroxide green from certification pursuant to section 721(c) of the act because certification is not necessary for public health protection.

asked: An older study suggests a colorant in our lip product (which may be ingested) caused tumors when fed to rats. How does FDA apply the cancer provision of section 721?
answer: The FDA applies section 721's cancer provision to your lip product by triggering 21 CFR 70.50(a) because the colorant may be ingested (as lips can be licked), and scientific data suggesting tumor induction in rats via ingestion meets the criteria for this subsection. Under 21 CFR 70.50(a), if scientific data suggests the color additive induces cancer when ingested by animals, FDA must determine whether cancer was induced and whether the additive caused it; if cancer has been induced, no regulation permitting its use may issue [1].

21 CFR 70.42(a) requires the presentation of all needed scientific data to assure that each listed color additive is safe for its intended use or uses in cosmetics [1].

21 CFR 70.42(c) requires a written request describing the proposed use of a color additive and the proposed experiments to determine its safety before the Commissioner advises whether planned experiments yield adequate data for evaluation [3].
